--- title: "Lesson 23 · Bayesian hypothesis testing and model comparison" subtitle: "Part V · Bayesian modeling" description: "Decisions with a region of practical equivalence, Bayes factors and Lindley's paradox, testing constrained hypotheses, and predictive model comparison with LOO." --- ::: {.meta-pills} [About 3.5 hours]{} [Before this: Lessons 6, 10 and 19–22]{} [Threads: uncertainty · frequentist ↔ Bayesian]{} [ ]{.pm-label} ::: ::: {.objectives} By the end of this lesson you will be able to - make decisions about effects with a posterior distribution and a region of practical equivalence; - compute and interpret a Bayes factor, and explain why it depends so strongly on the prior (Lindley's paradox); - test substantive, constrained hypotheses, such as an ordering of age-group effects; - compare models by their predictive accuracy with leave-one-out cross-validation, and read its diagnostics; - explain when Bayes factors and LOO disagree, and which question each answers. ::: ::: {.why} **Why it matters.** "Is there an effect?", "which hypothesis do the data favor?" and "which model predicts better?" are different questions, and the frequentist p-value of Lesson 6 answers none of them directly. Bayesian analysis offers a tool for each, but the tools behave very differently. A Bayes factor can flip from strong support for one hypothesis to strong support for the other just by widening a prior that looked harmless. Knowing why is part of using them responsibly. ::: ## 23.1 From posteriors to decisions: the region of practical equivalence {#s1} A posterior distribution already answers most questions about an effect. To decide whether an effect is **negligible**, define a **region of practical equivalence** (ROPE): effects too small to matter, here a few tenths of a percent change in visits per °C. If the 95% credible interval lies inside the ROPE, the effect is practically zero; if it lies entirely outside, it is meaningful; otherwise the data are undecided. This is the Bayesian counterpart of the equivalence test of Lesson 6. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$P(\beta \in \text{ROPE} \mid y) = P(-r < \beta < r \mid y)$$ ::: {.note} Decision rule: equivalent if the 95% credible interval lies inside $[-r, r]$; meaningful if it lies outside; otherwise undecided. ::: :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}How to read it ::: - $\text{ROPE}$: the region of practical equivalence: effects too small to matter. - $r$: the ROPE's half-width, fixed before seeing the data. - $\beta$: the effect. :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r draws <- posterior::as_draws_df(fit) b <- draws$b_heat mean(abs(b) < 0.003) # P(in ROPE) quantile(b, c(.025, .975)) # compare with ROPE ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#rReport} :::: ::::: ```{=html}
``` ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @kruschke2018rejecting introduces the ROPE decision rule; @kruschke2015doing on posterior decisions; @lakens2017equivalence on the frequentist equivalence test it parallels. ::: ## 23.2 Bayes factors and Lindley's paradox {#s2} A **Bayes factor** (sometimes called a "Bayesian factor") compares how well two hypotheses *predicted* the data before seeing them: the probability of the data under H₁ divided by that under H₀. For "no effect" (β = 0) against "some effect" (β drawn from a prior), it is easily computed as the ratio of the posterior and prior densities at zero (the **Savage–Dickey ratio**). The catch is that H₁'s prediction depends on its prior. A very wide prior spreads its bets over absurd effects, predicts the data poorly, and so loses to H₀, however small the p-value. This is **Lindley's paradox**. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$BF_{10} = \frac{p(y \mid H_1)}{p(y \mid H_0)} = \frac{p(\beta = 0 \mid H_1)}{p(\beta = 0 \mid y, H_1)} \quad \text{(Savage–Dickey)}$$ $$\text{normal case: } BF_{10} = \frac{\mathcal{N}(\hat\beta;\, 0,\, s^2 + \tau^2)}{\mathcal{N}(\hat\beta;\, 0,\, s^2)}$$ ::: {.note} $\hat\beta$, $s$: estimate and standard error; $\tau$: prior SD under H₁. Posterior odds = $BF_{10}$ × prior odds. ::: :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}How to read it ::: - $BF_{10}$: the Bayes factor for $H_1$ over $H_0$: how much better $H_1$ predicted the data. - $p(y \mid H_1)$: the marginal likelihood of $H_1$: its prediction of the data, averaged over its prior. - $p(\beta = 0 \mid H_1)$: the prior density at zero; divided by the posterior density at zero, it gives the Savage–Dickey Bayes factor. - $\hat\beta$: the estimate, with standard error $s$. - $\tau^2$: the prior variance under $H_1$: larger $\tau$ predicts larger effects, and penalizes $H_1$ if they don't appear. :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r brms::hypothesis(fit, "heat = 0") # Savage–Dickey # or marginal likelihoods for any two models: brms::bayes_factor(fit1, fit0) # bridge sampling ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#bReport} :::: ::::: ```{=html}
``` ::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfall"} Using default "vague" priors and then reporting a Bayes factor. For estimation, vague priors are often harmless; for Bayes factors, they are not neutral but decisive. A Bayes factor is only as meaningful as the prior under H₁, which should express a realistic range of effects (Lesson 20) and be reported with a sensitivity analysis. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): a Savage–Dickey Bayes factor by normal approximation"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summer65 <- visits |> filter(month(date) %in% 6:8, age_group == "65+") |> mutate(heat = temp - 22) fit <- glm(visits ~ heat + dow + district, family = quasipoisson, data = summer65) b <- coef(fit)["heat"]; s <- sqrt(vcov(fit)["heat", "heat"]) bf10 <- function(tau) dnorm(b, 0, sqrt(s^2 + tau^2)) / dnorm(b, 0, s) tibble(prior_sd_pct = c(0.5, 2, 10, 100)) |> mutate(BF10 = bf10(prior_sd_pct / 100), p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(b / s))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> # A tibble: 4 × 3 #> prior_sd_pct BF10 p_value #> #> 1 0.5 194269956. 2.16e-11 #> 2 2 377812380. 2.16e-11 #> 3 10 87356696. 2.16e-11 #> 4 100 8788436. 2.16e-11 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @kass1995bayes is the classic review of Bayes factors; @lindley1957statistical described the paradox; @wagenmakers2010bayesian explain the Savage–Dickey method; @jeffreys1961theory developed Bayes factors and their evidence scale. ::: ## 23.3 Testing substantive hypotheses {#s3} Bayes factors shine when the hypotheses are scientific statements rather than "zero vs not zero". Here are five hypotheses about how summer heat affects the three age groups: - **H₀:** no group is affected; - **H₌:** all groups are affected equally; - **Holder:** only older people (65+) are affected; - **Horder:** the effect increases with age (elderly > adults > children); - **Hᵤ:** no constraint. Order constraints are tested by comparing how much posterior and prior probability each hypothesis's region gets (the **encompassing prior** approach); equality constraints use the Savage–Dickey ratio. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$BF_{\text{order}, u} = \frac{P(\beta_{65+} > \beta_{15\text{–}64} > \beta_{0\text{–}14} \mid y, H_u)}{P(\beta_{65+} > \beta_{15\text{–}64} > \beta_{0\text{–}14} \mid H_u)}$$ ::: {.note} With exchangeable priors, the denominator is 1/6: each of the six orderings is equally likely before seeing the data. ::: :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}How to read it ::: - $BF_{\text{order}, u}$: the Bayes factor for the ordered hypothesis against the unconstrained model. - $\beta_{65+}$: the heat effect in the oldest group. - $H_u$: the unconstrained hypothesis. :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r brms::hypothesis(fit, "b_old > b_adult & b_adult > b_child") # informative hypotheses with bain: bain::bain(est, "old > adult > child", Sigma = vcov_est, n = n) ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#hReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @klugkist2005bayesian introduced encompassing priors for order-constrained hypotheses; @kass1995bayes on interpreting Bayes factors; @matthews1996interaction on why effects should be compared directly. ::: ## 23.4 Which model predicts better? LOO and how it differs from Bayes factors {#s4} **Leave-one-out cross-validation** (LOO) asks how well a model predicts each observation when that observation was left out of the fit. Summed over observations, this is the **expected log predictive density** (ELPD). Refitting the model n times would be prohibitive; **Pareto-smoothed importance sampling** (PSIS) approximates it from a single set of posterior draws, and its **Pareto k** values warn when the approximation fails. Here four models of daily visits by older Old Town residents are compared. The slider changes only the prior on the PM2.5 coefficient in model 3, and shows how differently LOO and the Bayes factor react. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$\mathrm{elpd}_{\text{loo}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log p(y_i \mid y_{-i}), \qquad p(y_i \mid y_{-i}) \approx \frac{\sum_s w_i^{(s)}\, p(y_i \mid \theta^{(s)})}{\sum_s w_i^{(s)}}$$ ::: {.note} $w_i^{(s)} \propto 1/p(y_i \mid \theta^{(s)})$, Pareto-smoothed. Values of $\hat k > 0.7$ flag unreliable estimates. ::: :::: :::: {.d} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}How to read it ::: - $\mathrm{elpd}_{\text{loo}}$: the expected log predictive density: how well the model predicts each observation when it is left out. - $p(y_i \mid y_{-i})$: the predictive density for observation $i$ from a model fitted without it. - $w_i^{(s)}$: importance weights that approximate leaving observation $i$ out, Pareto-smoothed in PSIS. - $p(y_i \mid \theta^{(s)})$: the likelihood of observation $i$ under draw $s$. :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r library(loo) loo1 <- loo(fit1); loo2 <- loo(fit2) loo_compare(loo1, loo2) # elpd_diff, se_diff plot(loo2) # Pareto k diagnostics ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [D]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#lReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Two questions, two tools"} A Bayes factor asks which model's **prior predictions** matched the data, so it judges the prior as part of the model. LOO asks which model's **posterior predictions** will work best for new data, so a vague prior that the data quickly overrule barely matters. Use Bayes factors when the hypotheses, including their priors, are scientific claims worth comparing; use LOO when the goal is prediction or choosing a working model. Stacking (combining models by weights that optimize LOO) is often better than choosing one. ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @vehtari2017practical introduced PSIS-LOO and its diagnostics; @yao2018using on stacking predictive distributions; @gronau2017tutorial on computing marginal likelihoods by bridge sampling. ::: ## Check your understanding {#quiz} ```{=html}
``` ## Key takeaways {#take} - With a posterior in hand, decide about effects with a region of practical equivalence: inside, outside or undecided. - A Bayes factor compares how well two hypotheses predicted the data. It depends strongly on the prior under the alternative: wide priors penalize it (Lindley's paradox). - Bayes factors are most useful for scientific hypotheses with realistic priors, such as ordered or constrained effects. - LOO compares models by predictive accuracy for new data; check Pareto k and the standard error of differences. - Bayes factors and LOO answer different questions, and can disagree. ## Concepts at a glance {#concepts} Ideas from this lesson that are easily confused, side by side. | Concept | What it is | How it differs | |---|---|---| | **ROPE** | A range of effects too small to matter. | Supports decisions: inside, outside or undecided. | | **Bayes factor** | How much better one hypothesis predicted the data than another. | Depends strongly on the prior; LOO doesn't, much. | | **Lindley's paradox** | A small p-value alongside a Bayes factor favoring the null. | Arises with wide priors and large samples. | | **LOO / ELPD** | Expected predictive accuracy for left-out observations. | Judges posterior predictions; Bayes factors judge prior predictions. | | **Pareto k** | A diagnostic for each observation's PSIS-LOO estimate. | Values above 0.7 need exact refits. | | **Stacking** | Weighting models' predictions to maximize LOO accuracy. | Combines models rather than choosing one. | ```{=html}
